issues.legal_issue: Other evidence cannot be used to prove a will under the fallback evidentiary rule when an available attesting witness has not been called and no attesting witness examined has denied or failed to recollect execution.
material_facts: The propounded will identified the claimant’s brother-in-law as an attesting witness, but he was not summoned or examined.
The claimant relied on the fact that the other alleged attesting witness, an advocate, had not been served and examined.
No attesting witness testified to denying or failing to recollect the will’s execution.
The High Court treated the will as proved through registration and other evidence.
issues.conclusion: The fallback rule for proving execution through other evidence was unavailable because the available attesting witness had not been examined and no examined attesting witness had denied or failed to recollect execution.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act and 68 and 71 of the Evidence Act require proof of a will through at least one attesting witness, if one is available and capable of giving evidence. Section 71 is a limited safeguard that applies when an attesting witness who has been called denies or cannot recollect execution; it does not excuse failure to call another available attesting witness. The Court relied on Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam, Jagdish Chand Sharma v. Narain Singh Saini, and Benga Behera v. Braja Kishore Nanda.

predicates.will_proof_dispute: A party seeks to establish a will in a dispute about its execution or validity.
predicates.available_attesting_witness_not_examined: The party relying on the will does not call an available attesting witness who can give evidence.
predicates.no_examined_attester_denied_or_forgot_ex: No attesting witness who was examined expressly denied execution or said that they could not recollect it.

issues.definition: When a will is disputed, the other-evidence fallback is unavailable if an available attesting witness is not examined and no examined attester denies or forgets the execution.

issues.legal_issue: A person’s signature on a will does not amount to attestation merely because the person drafted the document or performed a statutory registration function.
material_facts: The will bore the signature of an advocate whom the trial court regarded as having signed as draftsman and counsel, rather than as an attesting witness.
The registration official testified about the will’s registration, but the evidence did not establish that the official signed with the intention of attesting the testator’s signature.
The High Court relied in part on the advocate’s signature and the registration process in treating the will as attested by two witnesses.
issues.conclusion: Attestation requires the person to sign with the intention of witnessing the testator’s signature or acknowledgment; a signature made only in the course of drafting or performing a registration duty does not by itself satisfy that requirement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act requires attestation by two or more witnesses. Attestation requires animus attestandi: the witness must sign intending to attest that the executant signed or acknowledged the document. A registration officer’s statutory acts under Sections 52 and 58 of the Registration Act, 1908, do not by themselves make the officer an attesting witness; likewise, a draftsman or advocate is not an attesting witness merely by signing the document. The Court relied on Benga Behera v. Braja Kishore Nanda, Dharam Singh v. Aso, and Jagdish Chand Sharma v. Narain Singh Saini.

predicates.will_execution_disputed: A party disputes whether a will was executed and attested as required.
predicates.signature_made_only_for_drafting_or_regi: A person signed the document only while drafting it or performing a registration-related duty.
predicates.no_intention_to_attest: The person did not sign intending to witness the testator’s signature or acknowledgment.

issues.definition: In a disputed will, a signature made only for drafting or registration, without an intention to attest, does not count as attestation.

issues.legal_issue: A registered will is not proved by registration or other evidence when substantial suspicious circumstances remain unexplained by its propounder.
material_facts: The will was registered, but the testator was described as illiterate and the will contained unusual wording and a questionable description of the property and the transfer.
Before relying on the will in the suit, the beneficiary had claimed in response to a demand for partition that the property belonged to him absolutely, without referring to the will.
The evidence showed that the testator had received the allotment and that the beneficiary’s asserted ownership during her lifetime was at odds with the will’s stated bequest after her death.
The propounder did not remove the Court’s grave doubts about whether the testator and her family understood the nature of the document.
The propounder had not proved execution through an attesting witness, and the Court found the other evidence insufficient to prove execution.
issues.conclusion: The will was not proved through other evidence because registration did not resolve the substantial suspicious circumstances, which the propounder failed to remove; the High Court’s judgment was set aside and the trial court’s partition decree restored.
issues.legal_principle: The propounder must prove the will’s execution and, where circumstances raise legitimate suspicion, remove that suspicion before the will can be accepted. Registration is relevant but is not conclusive proof of due execution or a substitute for the statutory requirements of attestation and proof. Sections 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act and 68 and 71 of the Evidence Act apply. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur, Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam, M.B. Ramesh v. K.M. Veeraje Urs, and Jagdish Chand Sharma v. Narain Singh Saini.

predicates.will_proof_dispute: A party seeks to establish a will against a challenge to its execution or validity.
predicates.suspicious_execution_circumstances: The circumstances surrounding the will’s preparation or terms give reasonable grounds to doubt the testator’s understanding or free and informed execution.
predicates.propounder_failed_to_remove_suspicion: The party relying on the will does not adequately explain or dispel the reasonable doubts about its execution.

issues.definition: A disputed will is not proved when reasonable circumstances cast doubt on its execution and its propounder fails to dispel those doubts.
